lesson.title: Every Sample Imaginable: The Sampling Distribution of p-hat
lesson.summary: The sampling distribution of a proportion describes how the value of p-hat would vary across every possible sample of a given size, and it is the foundation for everything else in this unit.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter showed that a single sample produces a single value of p-hat, and a different sample would produce a different value. The sampling distribution of p-hat is the distribution of all those possible values, across every sample of size n that could have been drawn, each weighted by how likely it is to occur. It answers the question: if we could repeat this sampling process endlessly, what pattern would the resulting p-hat values trace out?

A small, fully enumerated example makes this exact rather than abstract. Imagine a tiny population of five marbles: two red and three blue. The true population proportion of red marbles is p = 2/5 = 0.4. Suppose we draw a simple random sample of two marbles, without replacement, and record p-hat, the proportion of red marbles in the sample. Label the marbles A and B (red) and C, D, E (blue). There are exactly ten equally likely samples of size two from five marbles: AB, AC, AD, AE, BC, BD, BE, CD, CE, DE.

Checking each one: AB contains two red marbles, so p-hat = 1. The six samples AC, AD, AE, BC, BD, and BE each contain exactly one red marble, so p-hat = 0.5 for each. The three samples CD, CE, and DE contain zero red marbles, so p-hat = 0 for each. Collecting this into a table, the sampling distribution of p-hat is: p-hat = 0 with probability 3/10, p-hat = 0.5 with probability 6/10, and p-hat = 1 with probability 1/10. Those three probabilities add to 10/10, confirming the enumeration is complete.

In real applications the population is far too large to enumerate every possible sample by hand, so we never build a table like this directly. Instead, statisticians rely on mathematical results about the shape, center, and spread of this distribution, which the next chapters develop. But the small marble example captures the essential idea exactly: the sampling distribution of p-hat is not one number, it is an entire distribution of possible outcomes, and everything we say about its mean and standard deviation in the coming chapters describes patterns in that full distribution, not any single sample.
